Rayed dosinia Dosinia exoleta is a venerid bivalve frequently encountered in subtidal sandy sediments of the northeastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. Field surveys indicate that the maximum recorded shell length for this species is 6 centimeters [Li = 6 centimeters], a dimension that defines the upper limit of adult size in local populations. Size-frequency distributions from dredge samples suggest that individuals requiring approximately 3.5 days [ab = approximately 3.5 days] to complete embryonic development under controlled laboratory conditions do so at a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], with the resulting eggs hatching into planktonic veliger larvae. The wet weight of a newly hatched larva, representing mass at birth, is estimated at 0.00000052 grams [Wwb = 0.00000052 grams], a figure derived from the calculated volume of the egg capsule assuming a diameter of roughly 100 micrometers. This extremely small initial biomass underscores the profound challenge of endogenous yolk provisioning during the brief lecithotrophic phase before the onset of planktotrophic feeding.

Populations of Dosinia exoleta inhabiting the English Channel exhibit a remarkably consistent growth trajectory that culminates in an ultimate wet weight of 30.85 grams [Wwi = 30.85 grams] for fully grown adults. This asymptotic body mass corresponds closely to the predicted value derived from the species' length-weight relationship and is attained after several years of sustained somatic expansion. The weight at which reproductive activity commences, corresponding roughly to the onset of gonadal maturation, has been estimated at 0.13 grams [Wwp = 0.13 grams] of live tissue mass. Delineating this pubertal threshold from field-collected individuals involves microscopic examination of gonadal smears to detect the earliest signs of gametogenic activity, a process that typically occurs when the shell has reached a much more modest length of approximately 1.2 centimeters [Lp = approximately 1.2 centimeters]. Reaching this size usually requires the bivalve to have survived the intense mortality bottleneck of the juvenile benthic recruit stage.

The reproductive schedule of Dosinia exoleta is tightly linked to seasonal temperature cycles, and under isothermal conditions maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] in the laboratory, a single gravid female can release an average of approximately 27,000 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 27,000 eggs per day] over the course of a spawning event. This daily reproductive output, which represents the maximum rate attainable by this species, reflects the prodigious fecundity typical of many venerid bivalves that rely on broadcast spawning in unpredictable coastal environments. Such high fecundity is an evolutionary response to extremely low larval survivorship, where fewer than one in a million eggs may successfully recruit to the benthic population.

Longevity records for Dosinia exoleta from shell growth lines and mark-recapture studies indicate that the species possesses a maximum lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years] when maintained at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] in stable subtidal environments. This extended lifespan is considerably greater than that reported for several other members of the family Veneridae of comparable ultimate shell size, suggesting a comparatively slow metabolic pace and a conservative life-history strategy adapted to resource-poor sedimentary habitats. Individuals that survive the initial post-settlement period typically enjoy a protracted adult phase characterized by repeated annual spawning events that gradually deplete somatic condition. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Dosinia lupinus reveal a similar pattern of delayed senescence, lending support to the hypothesis that the genus Dosinia is characterized by relatively low natural mortality rates once the vulnerable early life stages have been successfully traversed.

Variation in local environmental conditions, particularly food availability and sediment composition, can modulate the expression of key life-history traits in Rayed dosinia. For instance, individuals inhabiting organically enriched bays often achieve the pubertal shell length of 1.2 centimeters [Lp = 1.2 centimeters] at a considerably younger age than those dwelling in oligotrophic offshore sands, although the ultimate shell capacity does not surpass the species-wide maximum of 6 centimeters [Li = 6 centimeters]. Physiological studies have also noted that the age at which the fertilized egg emerges from its capsule, a developmental milestone fixed at approximately 3.5 days [ab = approximately 3.5 days] under standard laboratory conditions of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], can be slightly protracted at lower winter temperatures in the field, delaying the transition to the free-swimming veliger stage. Such plasticity, while modest in absolute terms, allows the species to buffer the impact of interannual climate variability on early life survival.
